newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: SAfrica committed to phasing out fx controls-Mbeki.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica committed to phasing out fx controls-Mbeki.

text.p: The South African government remains committed to the gradual elimination of exchange controls despite pressure on the rand, deputy president Thabo Mbeki said on Thursday.
He did not give any timescale for their removal, but said it was inevitable.
"The direction (of government policy) is quite clear, the commitment is quite firm," he told the Southern Africa Trade and Investment Summit being held in Harare.
Mbeki said the government was determined to meet growth targets laid down earlier this year in its macro-economic strategy to take the country into the next century.

The plan aims to double GDP growth to six percent a year, creating 400,000 new jobs a year by 2000. It is seen as vital in securing a peaceful and prosperous future for the country's fledgling democracy.
"These are targets we are determined to meet," Mbeki told the conference.
The government's macro-plan has won praise from business for its market-friendly policies, but earned some criticism from labour unions.
President Nelson Mandela's government is walking a tightrope between realising the demands of the black majority and not scaring away white South Africans and foreign business.
Mbeki said consensus was the way forward and those who called for quick reforms were overlooking the benefits of more gradual progress in improving the situation of the country's poorest people.
"The poor understand that it is not possible, within a day, to jump from a shack to a palace," he said.

Some investors worry that the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), South Africa's biggest labour group and an official ally of the government, wields too much influence over economic policy.

Mbeki said Cosatu and other unions, while having no power of veto, were a vital and constructive part of the consensus building process. "In practice these unions are not an obstacle to change and development, but an important partner in that process," he said.
